body_markdown:
The Pebble Beach Concours d’Elegance tends to be a busy week for everyone here at Hagerty Media. We cover a[significant amount of vehicles new and old](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/pebble-beach-concours-delegance/) , highlighting the scene from multiple viewpoints, and last week was no different. It’s safe to say we all get in a mood when the classics head to Monterey, and that mood is generally very elegant.


In the spirit of Pebble, I aksed our staff a very important question: *What’s your choice when considering a car with elegance?* Our team’s answers are something you likely won’t find fault with, but I am sure we didn’t cover them all. So have a look at our selections, and sound off with your selections for automotive elegance in the comments!


## Round Door Roller


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


“I think the 1925 Rolls-Royce Phantom I with body by Jonckheere. Also known as the ‘Round Door Rolls-Royce,’ this thing is an incredible piece of Art Deco styling and was legitimately breathtaking to see in person on the lawn at Pebble.” — *Greg Ingold*


## Buick’s Best


Buick


“I’ll concede that most prewar examples in this list take elegance to a higher degree than my Pabst-Blue-Ribbon taste could ever aspire. (I liked it before it became hipster beer, I swear.) For me, a Verde Green 1965 Buick Riviera is all the elegance I’ll ever need. One of the cleanest and most eye-catching designs ever to make it to production.” — *Eddy Eckart*


## Just kidding about the first one!


Chrysler


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


“No one ever has, or ever will, mention my name and ‘elegant’ in the same sentence. Growing up, I suppose Ricardo Montalban was all it took to convince me that the Chrysler Cordoba was elegant, so I’m an easy sell. *A rube, even.*


That said, I can’t look at a[1937 Cord 812](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-1937-cord-812-supercharged/) without thinking that the (few) people who bought that, or the essentially identical 810 model 90 years ago had to be among the most elegant people to ever walk the earth.” — *Steven Cole Smith*


## Aero-Elegance


Josh Sweeney


“I have a deep appreciation for the craftsmanship that went into early luxury cars and how elegant the final product became. My choice would be the[1935 Avions Voisin Type C25 Aérodyne](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/1935-voisin-c25-aerodyne-wins-best-in-show-at-2023s-amelia-concours-delegance/) . I might not have known this specific car existed until I saw it in photos from The Amelia in 2023 (where it went on to win best of show) and it’s stuck with me since. Lots of interesting little touches and to me that is true elegance.” — *Kyle Smith*


## The Classic Jaguar


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


“While my knee-jerk reaction would be to cite something like a 1930s Cadillac V-16 or a Duesenberg, those cars are so grandiose that I don’t think ‘elegance’ is the right descriptor. Instead, I think you need to have something a little bit dainty, something that manages to make simplicity look stunning.


This is a predictable pick, but I still think there is something so remarkable about the silhouette of the Jaguar E-Type Convertible. There’s a smoothness there in everything from the body’s shape to the way that the straight-six engine revs that I think captures ‘elegance’ perfectly.” — *Nathan Petroelje*


## French Elegance


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


“I think prewar French cars have always owned the elegance market. Tops among them all is a Talbot-Lago T150-C-SS from the late 1930s, with rear wheel spats but not front ones. That teardrop shape, and every line that contributes to it, is just perfect.” — *Stefan Lombard*


## The Elegant Bull


Lamborghini


“I’m leaning toward’s Nate’s definition of elegance. You don’t need a big car with bold lines to be elegant. That’s why my pick is the Lamborghini Miura.


Widely regarded as one of the most beautiful sports cars ever designed, as well as the origin of the supercar species, it’s a safe pick, yes, but in terms of supercar design it is remarkably simple and elegant. There are a few embellishments, yet compared to just about every supercar that followed that sought to cheat the wind while still cramming a huge volume of air to feed a hungry engine, the Miura effortlessly incorporates its ducts and scoops. It’s difficult to imagine that it came from the same company that produces the Urus.” — *Brandan Gillogly*


## The Graceful Giulia


Alfa Romeo


“I waited too long to submit my entry, and everyone already chosen my prewar faves! Therefore I have no choice but to take my revenge via a contrary stance: What if the most elegant classic car isn’t the most imposing one, but one that is both graceful and restrained?


I submit for your consideration the vintage Alfa Romeo Giulia. Pick any one of its variants other than the 2015 version (sorry): It embodies both qualities, with simple, neat styling and a driving experience that prioritizes precision and spirit over excess. Or so I hear. I haven’t driven one, and I really, really want to.” — *Grace Jarvis*


## Just kidding about the first one (Again)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Ronnie Schreiber](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rschreiber/)


“Much like the esteemed Steven Cole Smith, I am both old and yokel-enough to assume the personal luxury trend of the 1970s is a fantastic definition of elegance. That held true for a fair bit of time, but I wised up to the fact that the history of automotive elegance extends far past the Malaise Era.


I found the automobile section of my high school library (actually two libraries, that’s how big my school was!) in my sophomore year, and found a coffee table book with cars I would never see in my middle-class suburban neighborhood. And there it was: The Delage D8 120 Aerocoupe. I checked out that book so many times that I bet the librarian just assumed I’d grab it every time I walked in. My “if I won the lottery” taste in automobiles permanently shifted to a more rarified air with just one look of that magnificent creation.” — *Sajeev Mehta*
